candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classified this binary as malware with probability 0.885. All 20 top features push toward cryptojacking, and none pushes the other way. Together they add about +0.147 of SHAP contribution. The n-grams cluster into three families typical of hashing and proof-of-work arithmetic. (1) Rotate and shift bit-mixing: MOV ROL (+0.00997), ADD ROR (+0.00912), ROR MOV (+0.00847), ROL AND (+0.00807), SHL OR (+0.00662), ROL MOV (+0.00604), MOVZX ROL (+0.00590). (2) Multi-precision carry arithmetic and bit manipulation: SUB ADC (+0.00910), SHR ADC (+0.00641), ADC XOR (+0.00608), SUB NOT (+0.00607), BSWAP LEA (+0.00749), BSF MOV (+0.00611). (3) SSE/SIMD data shuffling and packed arithmetic: ADD MOVQ (+0.00923), MOVHLPS MOVQ (+0.00760), PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.00671), MOV PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.00595), MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.00584), MOVAPD DIVSD (+0.00762). The rotate-heavy patterns ADD ROR (freq 0.002919), ROR MOV (0.002258) and SHL OR (0.002189) are also among the most frequent n-grams in the binary, which fits a compute-intensive hashing loop. The case is strong but not conclusive. The evidence is purely mnemonic n-gram statistics with no function-level attribution, strings or API context. Most of the rare n-grams (frequency at or below 0.000005) are individually weak signals. Bit-rotation and carry-chain code also occurs in legitimate cryptographic, compression and checksum libraries. The consistency of all 20 features and the high model probability still support a high-confidence tier.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top-ranked feature. A load or move followed by a rotate-left is a typical round-function step in hash and cipher routines used for proof-of-work. Its frequency is very low (0.000071), so it is a sparse but highly discriminative marker.
Scalar addition adjacent to 64-bit XMM moves suggests mixed scalar/SIMD state handling, consistent with optimized mining kernels. Very rare (0.000031).

An add followed by a rotate-right is the classic add-rotate-xor pattern of ARX hash designs. At 0.002919 it is the most frequent top-ranked n-gram, which indicates repeated, loop-like execution of this pattern.
A subtract followed by add-with-carry indicates multi-word big-integer arithmetic, which appears in elliptic-curve and other crypto math. Frequency 0.000138.

A call immediately followed by a return indicates very small stub or thunk functions. This is a weak, ambiguous signal on its own, and the model weights it positively despite a very low frequency (0.000002). It adds little interpretable evidence without function context.
A rotate-right followed by a store or move is the continuation of a bit-mixing round. Its frequency (0.002258) is relatively high, which supports repeated hash-round code.
A rotate combined with a mask is typical of bit-field extraction and mixing in cryptographic primitives. Extremely rare (0.000002), but it carries a high SHAP weight.

A packed-double move followed by scalar double division is floating-point work. It is less obviously a hashing marker, but floating-point operations can appear in some mining algorithms or in difficulty and statistics handling. The evidence does not support a firm interpretation. Frequency 0.000001.
XMM high-to-low lane moves and 64-bit extraction are SIMD lane-manipulation steps used in vectorized hashing and AES-style state handling. Frequency 0.000157.
A byte-swap followed by address computation is endianness conversion, which is common when loading hash input or serializing digest output. Rare (0.000001).
Packed 64-bit addition with aligned 128-bit moves is vectorized arithmetic on wide state, consistent with SIMD-optimized hashing or memory-hard algorithm loops. Frequency 0.000179.
A shift-left combined with OR is manual rotate or bit-field composition, which supports the bit-mixing theme. Relatively frequent (0.002189).
A shift-right feeding add-with-carry is the carry-propagation pattern of big-integer or modular arithmetic. Frequency 0.000139.

A bit-scan-forward is used for bit-index and leading/trailing-zero logic, which can relate to difficulty or target checks, though it also appears in many general-purpose routines. Weak, low-frequency signal (0.000004).
Carry arithmetic combined with XOR mixes big-integer math with diffusion operations, a pattern common in cryptographic code. Rare (0.000005).
Subtraction followed by bitwise negation is a multi-precision or constant-time arithmetic idiom, also found in hash boolean functions. Rare (0.000002) and individually ambiguous.
A rotate-left followed by a move is another bit-rotation step in a hash round, reinforcing the rotate-heavy profile. Frequency 0.000075.
A move followed by a low-quadword unpack is SIMD lane interleaving, typical of vectorized state setup in optimized compute kernels. Frequency 0.000023.
A zero-extended byte or word load feeding a rotate suggests byte-wise input processing with rotation, as in hash message schedules. Frequency 0.000038.
A 64-bit XMM move followed by a quadword unpack is a SIMD data-packing idiom. With a frequency of 0.001955 it is relatively common in this binary, suggesting substantial vectorized processing.
